c91e725214f39495cc50576b0f9e7802195424ac.summary: A code-hosting page for a file in a public Python repository. The page lists folders (Amadey, Stealc, warzonerat) and files, including a notebook for extracting configuration from the WarzoneRAT malware family and a YARA rule file. It shows commit and archive metadata. It describes no actors, victims, campaigns or findings, so it is not a threat report.

c9af65927e7b013cfdb566cd32de2941c915ee0e.summary: eSentire's Threat Response Unit reports an opportunistic June 2021 malspam campaign by the FIN7 group, using a fake legal complaint about Brown-Forman. A law firm was a victim. The Excel lure installs the JSSLoader RAT via WMI. The report also covers FIN7's shifting lures, timed infrastructure registration, and suspected ties to Ryuk and REvil, which remain unconfirmed.

hedges: The role of one intermediate server is unclear; it may test whether a visitor is a susceptible victim rather than a security researcher.
The months-long gap before a landing page was used might have been meant to thwart reputation filters that use domain age.
The report calls the timing relative to the Brown-Forman claim deadline coincidental and says whether FIN7 is connected to the REvil attack remains to be seen.
Truesec theorized FIN7 may have sold access to the Ryuk group or may be closely affiliated with it; the report says either theory implies few sectors are out of scope.
A Swiss security company promised evidence linking FIN7 and REvil but never provided sufficient evidence, according to the report.
The report sees no apparent relationship between this infrastructure and infrastructure reported by previous research.
In-the-wild use of a newly registered lookalike domain has not been observed; the report assesses it will replace the prior one.
The report describes FIN7 selling initial access to ransomware groups as plausible, not confirmed.

c945838562918fd400a627b708e888d0b4c838d8.summary: CrowdStrike reports that two eCrime actors, SPRITE SPIDER (Defray777 ransomware) and CARBON SPIDER (Darkside ransomware), began deploying Linux versions of their ransomware in the second half of 2020, designed to encrypt VMware ESXi servers. The report calls this 'Hypervisor Jackpotting'. Both actors typically gain access with valid credentials to vCenter, then enable SSH for persistent access. The report expects more adversaries to target virtualization infrastructure in the medium term.

hedges: It is likely CARBON SPIDER pivoted to BGH in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
This likely reflects the overwhelming dominance of the Windows operating system in businesses and large organizations.
SPRITE SPIDER was relatively late to adopt the data-leak tactic, possibly due to a desire to avoid attention.
CARBON SPIDER likely began deploying Darkside to avoid sharing profits from BGH campaigns with PINCHY SPIDER.
It is likely that more adversaries will begin to target virtualization infrastructure in the medium term.
SPRITE SPIDER may delete the Defray777 binary after execution and may also uninstall VMware Fault Domain Manager.
The SHA256 hashes given are examples of the Linux variants only.
